notes.20:16: Where the Hebrew MT has a notoriously difficult closing phrase (often rendered "a covering of the eyes... you are completely vindicated"), the Greek reads "for the honor of your face and for all the women with you; and in all things speak the truth."
notes.20:18: The Greek renders the emphatic Hebrew verb construction as "closed up ... from the outside."
notes.21:9: The Greek text adds "with her own son Isaac," specifying with whom Ishmael was playing (absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text).
notes.21:14: Here and in vv. 32-33 (as well as 22:19), the Greek text translates the place name Beersheba as "the Well of the Oath" (and "Well of Swearing" in v. 31).
notes.21:16: The Greek text reads that the child cried out and wept rather than Hagar; similarly, v. 15 specifies "one fir tree" rather than a shrub, and v. 21 omits the name "Paran."
notes.21:33: The Greek renders the Hebrew word for "tamarisk tree" as "a field" (aroura, arable land); earlier, in vv. 22 and 32, the Greek also includes "Ahuzzath his bridal attendant" alongside Abimelech and Phicol (cf. 26:26).
notes.22:2: The Greek reads "your beloved son" (for Hebrew "your only one") and translates "the land of Moriah" as "the high land."
notes.22:3: The Greek places "on the third day" at the end of v. 3, attaching it to Abraham's arrival at the place rather than to the start of v. 4.
notes.22:13: The Greek reads "one ram" caught in "a sabek plant," transliterating the Hebrew word for "thicket" (sebak) as a plant name.
notes.22:24: The Greek text preserves the distinct name forms "Reera" (for Hebrew Reumah) and "Taam" (for Hebrew Gaham); in v. 21 it also renders "Aram" as "the Syrians."
notes.23:2: The Greek reads 'city of Arbok' (πόλει Ἀρβόκ) corresponding to Hebrew Kiriath-arba, and uniquely includes 'in the valley' (ἐν τῷ κοιλώματι, literally 'in the hollow').
notes.23:9: The Greek renders Hebrew Machpelah descriptively as 'the double cave' (τὸ σπήλαιον τὸ διπλοῦν; also in vv. 17, 19), reads 'in a portion' (ἐν μερίδι) rather than 'at the end', and uses the plural imperative 'give' (δότε).
notes.23:13: The Greek text reads the second-person imperative 'bury' (θάψον) rather than the first-person future 'I will bury' (cf. v. 4 and the Hebrew text).
notes.23:15: The Greek reads 'for I have heard' (ἀκήκοα γάρ) without explicitly mentioning 'land', and specifies the currency as 'didrachmas' (δίδραχμα; also in v. 16) rather than Hebrew shekels.
notes.24:7: The Greek text reads "the God of heaven and the God of the earth" and "To you I will give this land and to your seed," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text omits "and the God of the earth" and "to you."
notes.24:22: The Greek reads plural "gold earrings, each a drachma in weight," whereas the Hebrew has a single gold nose-ring weighing half a shekel.
notes.24:24: The Greek phrasing "whom she bore to him, Nahor" uses an appositional dative (αὐτῷ Ναχώρ) identifying Nahor as the father to whom Milcah bore Bethuel.
notes.24:26: The Greek participle εὐδοκήσας ("being pleased") differs from the Hebrew "bowed his head."
notes.24:31: The Greek reads nominative εὐλογητὸς Κύριος ("Blessed is the Lord") as an exclamation of praise, rather than the Hebrew "blessed of the Lord" addressed to the servant.
notes.24:36: The Greek reads "one son" and "after he had grown old" (masculine αὐτόν, referring to Abraham), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "a son" and "after her old age" (referring to Sarah).
notes.24:50: The Greek idiom ἀντειπεῖν κακὸν καλῷ ("speak against you evil for good") differs from the Hebrew "speak to you bad or good."
notes.24:59: The Greek reads "her possessions" (τὰ ὑπάρχοντα αὐτῆς), whereas the Hebrew has "her nurse."
notes.24:62: The Greek renders the place name Beer-lahai-roi descriptively as "the Well of Vision" (τὸ φρέαρ τῆς ὁράσεως) and adds "through the wilderness."
notes.24:67: The Greek reads "Isaac entered the house of his mother" and ends with "concerning Sarah his mother," whereas the Hebrew reads "brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother" and "after his mother."
notes.25:3: The Greek text includes Teman among Jokshan's sons and adds Reuel and Nabdeel among Dedan's sons, along with Datusieim (where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Letushim).
notes.25:4: The Greek text reads the distinct names Gephar, Abira, and Thergama (where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Ephah, Abida, and Eldaah).
notes.25:15: In verses 13-15, the Greek text preserves the distinct name forms Nabdeel, Iduma, Choddan, and Teman (where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Adbeel, Dumah, Hadad, and Tema).
notes.25:18: The Greek text reads Suel where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Shur.
notes.26:10: Greek agnoian literally means "ignorance," used in the Septuagint for an unwitting sin or cultic guilt (corresponding to Hebrew "guilt").
notes.26:12: The Greek text specifies "a hundredfold of barley," reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants ("barley" rather than "measures").
notes.26:32: The Greek text explicitly reads "We did not find water" (ouch heuromen hydor), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "We have found water."
notes.26:34: The Greek text identifies Elon as "the Hivite" (rather than "the Hittite" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text), and in verse 35 describes Esau's wives as "quarreling" with Isaac and Rebekah.
notes.27:12: Greek "ὡς καταφρονῶν" ("as one showing contempt") renders the sense of a mocker or deceiver as someone treating his father with disdain.
notes.27:29: The Septuagint reads "rulers" (for Hebrew "peoples"), singular "your brother," and "the sons of your father" (where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the sons of your mother").
notes.27:36: "Tripped me up" renders Greek "ἐπτέρνικεν" (literally, "struck at the heel" or "supplanted"), preserving the wordplay on the name Jacob.
notes.27:39: The Greek preposition "ἀπό" ("from") mirrors the phrasing of 27:28 and can be understood either as source ("from the richness") or separation ("away from the richness").
notes.28:3: The Septuagint reads "my God" rather than "God Almighty" (Hebrew El Shaddai).
notes.28:10: The Septuagint translates the place name Beersheba literally as "the Well of the Oath."
notes.28:14: The Septuagint compares Jacob's offspring to "the sand of the sea" (Hebrew Masoretic Text: "the dust of the earth") and lists the compass directions as sea (west), south, north, and east.
notes.28:19: The Septuagint translates Bethel as "House of God" and gives the city's former name as "Oulammaus," which reflects a conflation of the Hebrew particle "ulam" ("however") with the city name "Luz."
notes.29:1: The Septuagint expands Jacob's destination beyond the Hebrew text by adding "to Laban the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau"; Greek "Syrian" (Syros) regularly translates Hebrew "Aramean."
notes.29:6: Unlike the Hebrew text, where the shepherds point out Rachel's arrival, the Septuagint shifts to narration with "While he was still speaking" and anticipates the description of Rachel approaching with her father's sheep repeated in verse 9.
notes.29:20: The Septuagint concludes the verse here without the clause present in the Masoretic Text ("and they seemed to him like a few days because of his love for her").
notes.29:27: Greek "ta hebdoma" (literally "the sevens") refers to the seven-day bridal week of Leah's wedding celebration.
notes.29:34: Greek "pros emou" ("on my side" or "attached to me") reflects the Hebrew wordplay on Levi ("joined"), and the Septuagint uses the passive verb "was called" rather than "she called."
notes.30:8: The Septuagint reads "God has helped me, and I have contended with my sister" (συνεβάλετό μοι ὁ θεός, καὶ συνανεστράφην τῇ ἀδελφῇ μου), rendering the Naphtali wordplay differently from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "with mighty wrestlings I have wrestled."
notes.30:15: The Septuagint reads "Not so" (οὐχ οὕτως), reflecting a different vocalization or reading of the Hebrew consonant group that the Masoretic Text reads as "Therefore" (laken).
notes.30:27: The Septuagint construes οἰωνισάμην ἄν ("I would have observed omens") as the potential conclusion to "If I have found favor before you," whereas the Masoretic Text treats the verb as a statement ("I have learned by divination").
notes.30:32: The Septuagint has Jacob instruct Laban with "Let your sheep pass by today, and separate from there," whereas the Masoretic Text has Jacob speak in the first person ("Let me pass through all your flock today, removing from there").
notes.30:42: In vv. 41-42 the Septuagint contrasts when the sheep were "conceiving" versus "giving birth," and calls the resulting offspring "unmarked" (ἄσημα) and "marked" (ἐπίσημα), diverging from the Masoretic Text's "stronger" and "feebler" flocks.
notes.31:7: Greek ton deka amnon ("of the ten lambs"; cf. deka amnasin, "ten ewe-lambs," in v. 41) reflects the Septuagint reading of the Hebrew expression elsewhere rendered "ten times."
notes.31:33: The Septuagint uses oikos ("house") rather than "tent" in vv. 33–37 and orders Laban's search differently from the Masoretic Text, beginning with Leah's house before Jacob's and that of the two female servants.
notes.31:47: Rather than transliterating the Aramaic and Hebrew names (Jegar-sahadutha and Galeed), the Septuagint translates both into Greek as Bounos martys ("Witness Heap") and Bounos martyrei ("Heap Testifies").
notes.31:49: The Septuagint translates the place name Mizpah into Greek as He horasis ("The Vision"); in this Greek text, the material corresponding to Masoretic v. 51 is integrated into vv. 48–50 and 52, so verse numbering skips from v. 50 to v. 52.
notes.32:2: The Greek includes "looking up with his eyes, he saw a camp of God encamped" before the angels meet Jacob, and in 32:3 translates Hebrew Mahanaim as Parembolai ("Camps").
notes.32:11: The Greek reads hikanousai moi ("You are sufficient for me", a textual variant alongside hikanoutai moi, "it is enough for me") where the Hebrew text reads "I am unworthy of all the steadfast love and faithfulness."
notes.32:26: The Greek describes "the flat of his thigh" growing "numb" (enarkesen, also in 32:33) rather than being dislocated as in the Hebrew text.
notes.32:31: The Greek translates Hebrew Peniel as Eidos theou ("Appearance of God", and "the Appearance of God" in 32:32), creating a wordplay with eidon ("I saw").
notes.33:14: The Greek reads "I will gain strength (enischyso) along the way at the leisurely pace of the journey," differing from the Hebrew idiom "I will lead on slowly."
notes.33:17: The Greek translates Hebrew Succoth as Skenai ("Tents"), echoing the tents made for Jacob's livestock, and reads plural "houses" rather than singular "house."
notes.33:18: The Greek takes Hebrew shalem ("safely") as a proper name, "Salem, a city of Shechem," and renders Paddan-aram as "Mesopotamia of Syria."
notes.33:19: The Greek reads "from Hamor the father of Shechem" (without "the sons of") and renders the monetary unit Hebrew qesitah as "lambs."
notes.33:20: The Greek reads "called upon the God of Israel" (epekalesato ton theon Israel) rather than naming the altar El-Elohe-Israel as in the Hebrew text.
notes.34:2: The Greek text identifies Hamor as "the Horite" (Χορραῖος), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Hivite."
notes.34:14: The Greek text explicitly names Simeon and Levi, the brothers of Dinah and sons of Leah, as the speakers, whereas the Hebrew text leaves the subject unspecified.
notes.34:15: The Greek verb rendered "become like" (ὁμοιόω, also in vv. 22-23) translates a Hebrew verb meaning "consent," emphasizing assimilation into one people.
notes.34:29: The Greek terms σώματα ("persons") and ἀποσκευή ("dependents") reflect Hellenistic usage for captives and non-combatant household members; the Greek also adds "whatever was in the city" to the plunder.
notes.35:4: The concluding clause "and destroyed them until the present day" is present in the Greek text but absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.35:11: The Greek reads "your God" (ὁ θεός σου) rather than the Hebrew "God Almighty" (El Shaddai), and uses the plural "nations and assemblies of nations."
notes.35:16: In the Greek text, Jacob's pitching of his tent beyond the tower of Gader (Hebrew: Eder) appears here rather than at v. 21, which is absent in Greek; "Chabratha" transliterates the Hebrew term for a short measure of distance.
notes.35:22: The clause "and it appeared evil before him" completes the sentence in the Greek text, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text breaks off after "Israel heard."
notes.35:27: The Greek renders the Hebrew place name Kiriath-arba as "the city of the plain" (πόλιν τοῦ πεδίου).
notes.36:2: The Greek text identifies Anah as 'the son of Zibeon' (likewise in 36:14), aligning with 36:24-25, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'the daughter of Zibeon'.
notes.36:21: The Greek text names Seir's last two sons Saar and Rison (repeated in 36:27-30, where Saar is given four sons: Bilhan, Zukam, Jukam, and Ukan), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Ezer (with three sons) and Dishan.
notes.36:24: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to Anah finding 'the hot springs' (or an uncertain term) while tending donkeys, the Greek reads 'Onan / Onas' finding a person named 'Jamin' while pasturing beasts of burden.
notes.36:31: This Greek text reads 'in Jerusalem', a manuscript reading distinct from the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most Septuagint witnesses, which read 'in Israel' (or 'over the Israelites').
notes.36:32: The Greek reads Balak (Βάλακ) here and in 36:33 where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has Bela; this Edomite king is distinct from Balak king of Moab in Numbers 22–24.
notes.36:39: The Greek text names this king 'Arath the son of Barath' (with city Peor and Matred as 'the son of Me-zahab'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'Hadar' without a patronymic (with city Pau and 'daughter of Me-zahab'); several other names in this chapter also reflect distinct Greek forms (Zophar in 36:11, 15; Balak in 36:32; Barad and Gethaim in 36:35; Jeber, Phines, Metodiel, and Zaphoi in 36:40-43).
notes.37:2: The Greek text uses a plural verb ('they brought an evil accusation against Joseph to Israel their father'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text makes Joseph the subject bringing a bad report about his brothers.
notes.37:28: The Greek text specifies 'twenty gold pieces' (εἴκοσι χρυσῶν), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads twenty pieces of silver.
notes.37:36: The Greek renders Potiphar's titles as 'eunuch' (σπάδοντι) and 'chief cook' (ἀρχιμαγείρῳ), reflecting a literal rendering of the Hebrew root for slaughtering/cooking rather than 'captain of the guard.'
notes.38:2: Using the feminine relative pronoun (ᾗ), the Greek identifies Shua as the name of Judah's Canaanite wife (cf. 38:12), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text makes Shua the name of her father.
notes.38:5: The Greek reads 'she was in Chezib when she gave birth to them' (plural), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('he was in Chezib when she bore him').
notes.38:12: The Greek identifies Hirah as Judah's 'shepherd' (ποιμήν; also in 38:20), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants than the Masoretic Text's 'friend.'
notes.38:29: The Greek renders the Hebrew wordplay on the name Perez ('breach') with the verb 'was broken through' (διεκόπη) and the noun 'barrier' or 'fence' (φραγμός).
notes.39:1: The Greek reads "eunuch" (εὐνοῦχος) and "chief cook" (ἀρχιμάγειρος), reflecting the Septuagint's literal rendering of titles often translated from the Hebrew as "officer" and "captain of the guard."
notes.39:8: The Greek opens Joseph's reply with conditional "If" (εἰ), rendering the Hebrew interjection hen ("look") as a conditional clause answered by "then how..." in verse 9.
notes.39:12: Throughout verses 12-18, the Greek uses the plural "garments" (τὰ ἱμάτια) where the Hebrew has the singular "garment," and omits "in her hand" here while retaining it in verse 13.
notes.39:20: The Greek renders Joseph's place of confinement here and in 40:14 as "stronghold" (ὀχύρωμα), distinct from "prison" (δεσμωτήριον) in 39:22 and 40:3, 5.
notes.40:4: The Greek uses the rare compound ἀρχιδεσμώτης ("chief warden") here, varying from ἀρχιδεσμοφύλαξ ("chief jailer") in 39:21-23 and 40:3.
notes.40:5: The Greek reads "a vision of his dream" (ὅρασις τοῦ ἐνυπνίου αὐτοῦ), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "each according to the interpretation of his dream."
notes.40:13: Here and in verse 20, the Greek reads "remember your office" (μνησθήσεται τῆς ἀρχῆς σου), interpreting the Hebrew idiom "lift up your head."
notes.40:16: The Greek χονδριτῶν refers specifically to loaves made of coarse wheat or groats, where the Hebrew has "baskets of white bread" or "perforated baskets."
notes.41:16: The Greek literally reads "Apart from God, the welfare of Pharaoh will not be answered," differing from the Hebrew text ("It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer").
notes.41:38: Greek pneuma theou ("spirit of God," without the article) can be understood either as a divinely given spirit or as "the Spirit of God" (compare Gen 1:2).
notes.41:45: The Greek preserves distinct forms for the Egyptian names: "Psonthomphanech" (Hebrew "Zaphenath-paneah"), "Petrephe" (Πετρεφῆ, rendered with standard English "Potiphera" as in 46:20; most Greek witnesses read "Petephres"), and "Heliopolis" ("City of the Sun," rendering Hebrew "On").
notes.41:48: This Greek text contains the name "On" after "around it," likely an early gloss identifying the city or an uncial misreading of a relative pronoun.
notes.41:52: This Greek text reads "exalted" (Greek hypsosen) rather than the more common Septuagint reading "increased/made fruitful" (euxesen), forming a direct contrast with "humiliation."
notes.41:54: This Greek text reads "there was no bread" (Greek ouk esan artoi), whereas the Hebrew text and other Greek witnesses state that "there was bread" in all the land of Egypt.
notes.42:4: The Septuagint reads "illness" (μαλακία, and similarly "falls ill" in 42:38) rather than the Masoretic Text's "harm" or "mischief."
notes.42:9: The Septuagint renders this phrase as "the tracks of the country" (τὰ ἴχνη τῆς χώρας, and "tracks of the land" in 42:12), interpreting the Hebrew idiom for the land's vulnerable spots ("nakedness").
notes.42:11: The Septuagint translates the brothers' self-description as "peaceable" (εἰρηνικοί; also in 42:19, 31, 33, 34), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "honest."
notes.42:15: The Septuagint oath "by the health of Pharaoh" (νὴ τὴν ὑγίαν Φαραώ; also in 42:16) corresponds to "by the life of Pharaoh" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.42:38: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew "Sheol" (the realm of the dead) as "Hades" (ᾅδου).
notes.43:11: The Septuagint lists "terebinth" (τερέμινθον) and "walnuts" (κάρυα) among the gifts, corresponding to "pistachios" and "almonds" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.43:14: The Septuagint reads "my God" (ὁ θεός μου) where the Masoretic Text reads "God Almighty" (El Shaddai).
notes.43:23: The steward's greeting "Be at ease" translates the Greek idiom ἵλεως ὑμῖν (literally "gracious/merciful to you"), rendering the Hebrew greeting of peace.
notes.43:28: The sentence "And he said, 'Blessed is that man by God'" is present in the Septuagint and not found in the Masoretic Text.
notes.43:32: The Septuagint specifies "for every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians" (matching Genesis 46:34), whereas the Masoretic Text reads simply "for that is an abomination to the Egyptians."
notes.44:5: The question "Why did you steal my silver cup?" is a Septuagint addition not in the Masoretic Text; in the Greek source, the verse division splits the idiom hina ti ("why") between 44:4 and 44:5.
notes.44:18: Greek reads meta Pharao ("after Pharaoh," i.e., second only to Pharaoh), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "like Pharaoh."
notes.44:28: Greek reads second-person plural eipate ("you said"), attributing the words to the brothers, where the Masoretic Text has first-person singular ("I said").
notes.44:29: Greek renders Hebrew "harm" with malakia ("sickness" or "infirmity") and "Sheol" with Haidou ("Hades," also in 44:31).
notes.45:3: In this Greek text, "your brother, whom you sold into Egypt" already appears in verse 3, and verse 4 omits Joseph's invitation for the brothers to draw near.
notes.45:10: Greek Gesem Arabias ("Goshen of Arabia") adds the geographical qualifier "of Arabia" to Goshen.
notes.45:14: This Greek text reads epepesen ep' auto ("he fell upon him") rather than "he wept upon him" as in other Septuagint witnesses and the Masoretic Text.
notes.45:17: Greek poria denotes carts or conveyances, corresponding to Hebrew "beasts."
notes.45:22: Greek reads triakosious chrysous ("three hundred gold pieces"), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "three hundred pieces of silver."
notes.46:10: The Greek genealogy preserves several Septuagint-distinct personal names where the Masoretic Hebrew text differs, including Samuel here (Hebrew Shaul), Jemuel in v. 12 (Hamul), Zambram in v. 13 (Shimron), Hezron in v. 14 (Elon), Thasoban in v. 16 (Ezbon), Jessai and Jeul in v. 17 (Ishvah and Ishvi), and Chobor in v. 21 (Becher).
notes.46:20: The Septuagint expands Joseph's genealogy with five additional descendants through Manasseh and Ephraim (Machir, Gilead, Sutalaam, Taam, and Edem; cf. Num 26:29–36), which contribute to the larger totals in vv. 22 and 27.
notes.46:27: The Septuagint counts nine souls born to Joseph in Egypt and seventy-five total for Jacob's house (the figure cited in Acts 7:14), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew text counts two and seventy.
notes.46:28: The Septuagint names the meeting place Heroonpolis (Greek Heroon polis, "City of Heroes") in the land of Rameses, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew text reads Goshen.
notes.46:34: The Septuagint specifies "Goshen of Arabia," referring to the eastern Egyptian border nome known in Hellenistic geography as Arabia, where the Hebrew reads simply "Goshen."
notes.47:4: In this Greek text, Pharaoh's grant of Goshen and his instruction about capable men come within verse 4, before the notice that Jacob and his sons arrived in Egypt and that Pharaoh heard; Pharaoh's address to Joseph follows in verses 5-6.
notes.47:18: The Greek verb ektribomen ("be wiped out") interprets the underlying Hebrew root k-ch-d in the sense of destruction rather than concealment ("hide from my lord" in the Masoretic text).
notes.47:19: The Greek source text has no negative particle before the final future verb, reading literally "and the land will become desolate" rather than "and the land will not become desolate."
notes.47:21: The Septuagint reads "enslaved the people to him as servants" (agreeing with the Samaritan Pentateuch), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew text reads "removed them to the cities."
notes.47:31: The Septuagint reads "upon the top of his staff" (quoted in Heb 11:21), reflecting the vocalization matteh ("staff") rather than the Masoretic mittah ("bed").
notes.48:3: The Greek reads "my God," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "God Almighty" (El Shaddai).
notes.48:7: The Greek renders the Hebrew distance phrase (kibrat ha-aretz) with both the gloss "the racecourse" (hippodromos) and the transliteration "Chabratha."
notes.48:22: The Greek treats the Hebrew word for "ridge" or "portion" (shekhem) as the city name Shechem (Sikima), confirmed by the feminine relative pronoun "which" (hen).
notes.49:6: The Greek reads "my liver" (ta hepata mou), reflecting a reading of the Hebrew consonants as kaved ("liver") rather than kavod ("glory").
notes.49:10: The Greek reads "the things reserved for him" (ta apokeimena auto), understanding the Hebrew Shiloh as shelo ("that which belongs to him"), and renders the final clause as "the expectation of nations."
notes.49:14: The Greek reads "desired what is good" rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "a strong donkey," and translates the final noun as "allotments" (kleroi).
notes.49:21: The Greek reads the Hebrew consonants as a "trunk" (stelechos) yielding beauty in its produce, rather than the Masoretic Text's "doe let loose" bearing beautiful fawns.
notes.49:24: The Greek reads "their bows were shattered with might" and "the one who strengthened Israel" (ho katischysas Israel, which may be understood either as a divine title parallel to "the Mighty One of Jacob," i.e., "the One who strengthened Israel," or as referring to Joseph), differing from the Masoretic Text's "his bow remained steady" and "the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel."
notes.50:3: The Greek reads a singular active verb with a plural object ("he completed forty days for them"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads passively ("forty days were fulfilled for him").
notes.50:11: The Septuagint translates the place name into Greek (Πένθος Αἰγύπτου, "Mourning of Egypt") rather than transliterating the Hebrew Abel-mizraim.
notes.50:13: The Septuagint renders Hebrew Machpelah descriptively as "the double cave" (τὸ σπήλαιον τὸ διπλοῦν) and specifies "the cave" rather than "the field" as the property Abraham acquired.
notes.50:19: The Septuagint renders Joseph's response as a statement ("for I belong to God," τοῦ γὰρ θεοῦ ἐγὼ εἰμί), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has a rhetorical question ("Am I in the place of God?").
notes.50:26: The Greek verb ἔθαψαν ("buried" or "prepared for burial") corresponds here to the Hebrew verb for embalming, followed by Joseph's placement in the coffin in Egypt.
